highlights.content: Google launched Gemini 4 Neon on November 18 — its fourth Gemini 4 model in seven weeks, priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It debuted #1 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, scored 61 on the AA Intelligence Index at its highest thinking setting, and reportedly matched Claude Opus 5.5 on a real coding benchmark at less than half the cost per task. > 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap → Those numbers matter. But they are not the story. The story is that the leaderboard has fractured so completely that four labs can each claim #1 on a different index — and that Google is using price, not performance, as the weapon that actually moves markets. *View original announcement on Google Blog →* ## Four Models, Seven Weeks Here is what Google shipped in the Gemini 4 family since late September: | Model | Date | Role | Pricing (per 1M tokens) | |---|---|---|---| | **Gemini 4 Argon** | Sep 30 | Deep reasoning, frontier intelligence | $2 / $10 (intro) → $4 / $20 after Nov 30 | | **Gemini 4 Carbon** | Oct 28 → Nov 10 (GA) | Most complex work, cybersecurity | $2 / $10 (intro) → $4 / $20 after Nov 30 | | **Gemini 4 Hydrogen** | Nov 12 | Speed tier, cheapest frontier | $1.50 / $0.75 | | **Gemini 4 Neon** | Nov 18 | Coding agents, knowledge work | $3 / $15 | That is a new model roughly every 12 days. No other lab has matched this shipping velocity in 2026. Anthropic's last major release was Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22 — nearly two months ago. OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17, the day before Neon, and the consensus across YouTube and Substack is that it "got slept on." We covered the Carbon/Hydrogen double-launch last week. The pattern continues: Google is not trying to win one benchmark cycle. It is trying to make the benchmark cycle irrelevant by shipping faster than anyone can evaluate. ## The Pricing Game The benchmarks are close enough to argue about. The pricing is not. highlights.title: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
highlights.titleZh: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
highlights.content: The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole. But while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there's still a paradox at the heart of Washington's AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction. The Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president's vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn't just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too. Today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global users. Chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones. The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration's dreams of AI dominance is that success at one layer of the stack is undermining its goals at another. When people hear that Chinese models are gaining users, they generally assume that those models are running on Chinese chips. While that's increasingly the case within China, the truth is that China cannot produce enough advanced AI chips to satisfy its own companies, let alone meet overseas demand. Meanwhile, America's grip on AI infrastructure is formidable. U.S. companies—Nvidia, Google, AMD, and Amazon—design nearly all deployed data-center AI chips. In cloud services, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google together control more than half of the market, with a growing cohort of U.S. "neoclouds" further extending that lead. Yet the same infrastructure that secures America's advantage in chips and cloud services gives Chinese AI models a platform to spread. Nvidia itself provides resources to help companies deploy open models—including several Chinese models—on its hardware. U.S.-based model inference providers such as Together AI, Baseten, and Fireworks serve Chinese models to users on infrastructure powered by U.S. chips. For example, DeepSeek's latest model is being offered by at least 16 inference providers headquartered outside China, including Amazon Bedrock.

highlights.content: # The Future of Nvidia: Still the AI King, But the Crown Is Getting Heavier Nvidia’s extraordinary run as the dominant force in artificial intelligence hardware shows no immediate sign of ending. Yet the company finds itself at an inflection point. Record demand collides with a sudden leadership vacuum, intensifying competition and growing questions about how long the current spending frenzy can last. The near-term outlook remains robust; the longer-term picture is more contested. In the third quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, Nvidia delivered another set of results that would once have seemed implausible. Revenue reached $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure, while data-centre sales climbed 110 per cent to $107.6 billion. The new Vera Rubin platform contributed nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. Management guided the following quarter to approximately $130 billion and raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to around 75 per cent, from a previous 70 per cent, on a higher base. Supply commitments have swollen to roughly $390 billion and visibility into customer demand stretches into 2029 in several cases. Cloud industry backlog is reported at $2.5 trillion. These numbers explain why many analysts continue to describe the stock, even after a sharp pullback, as reasonably valued against the growth still on offer. ### The Leadership Shock The most dramatic recent development has been the resignation of founder and long-time chief executive Jensen Huang. On 12 November 2026 he stepped down with immediate effect as president, chief executive and a member of the board, after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded. The departure followed reports of extramarital affairs, one involving a businesswoman whom United States intelligence agencies suspected of links to Chinese intelligence, and another with a Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. The board accepted the resignation and has since stated clearly that it does not intend to reinstate him. Colette Kress, the long-serving chief financial officer, was appointed interim chief executive and continues in both roles while a permanent successor is sought. Harvey C. Jones was named the company’s first-ever board chair. For now, executives insist that operations continue as normal. The product roadmap — Rubin Ultra expected in 2027, followed by the next generation thereafter — remains intact. Whether a new permanent leader can match Huang’s combination of technical vision, salesmanship and industry relationships is the open question that will shape the next chapter. ### Competition Is Catching Up Nvidia still commands the large majority of the high-end AI accelerator market. Its CUDA software ecosystem and full-stack approach — chips, networking, systems and software — create formidable switching costs. That advantage is real and enduring. Yet the competitive landscape is shifting. Advanced Micro Devices has steadily increased its share. Hyperscalers are accelerating development and deployment of their own specialised chips: Google’s tensor processing units, Amazon’s Trainium processors and Microsoft’s custom silicon. As workloads move from pure model training towards inference and more specialised tasks, alternatives become more viable. Tools that ease the migration of models away from CUDA are improving. Export controls have already sharply reduced Nvidia’s China exposure. Further restrictions remain a risk. Power constraints, data-centre financing and customer concentration add further potential pressure points. ### The Cycle Question The most important longer-term uncertainty is the durability of AI infrastructure spending itself. highlights.title: If AI Chips Become Commoditized, Nvidia Has the Most to Lose, While These 3 Stocks Are Set to Gain
highlights.titleZh: If AI Chips Become Commoditized, Nvidia Has the Most to Lose, While These 3 Stocks Are Set to Gain
highlights.content: The AI chip market is starting to shift, and with it, **Nvidia**'s (NASDAQ:NVDA) grip. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model could start running part of its AI models on alternative AI chips to Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a process that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. This greatly reduces Nvidia's CUDA moat at a time when competitors are starting to catch up. **Alphabet**'s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) have started to outperform Nvidia's GPUs on a performance-per-dollar basis, according to Semianalysis (though some dispute the results). Meanwhile, **Advanced Micro Devices**' (NASDAQ:AMD) GPUs continue to gain traction. The company has improved its software stack, and its chips' larger memory capacity makes them ideal for inference. *Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout.* Continue » Image source: Getty Images. If the gap between AI chips continues to shrink and AI models can be quickly shifted to run on any AI accelerator, this is very bad news for Nvidia. Not only will the company continue to lose market share, but, more importantly, its pricing power will erode, and its margins will shrink. The Nvidia premium can be seen in its gross margins, which are in the mid-70% range, versus AMD's in the mid-50% range. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of **SpaceX** (NASDAQ:SPCX), have been developing their own custom AI chips to try to break free of Nvidia's high prices. All is not lost for Nvidia, as the company still holds some advantages. It has created a cohesive hardware, software, and networking ecosystem that should still be able to command a premium. It also has major current supply chain advantages, having locked up more access to constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) supply and having more manufacturing and packaging capacity with **Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing** (NYSE:TSM). That will help it maintain its leadership position, even as it will likely face continued market-share and pricing pressure. While Nvidia may struggle, these three AI stocks look set to benefit. ## Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Lower AI accelerator prices and more Nvidia GPU alternatives could boost overall AI chip demand, which would benefit Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. It would also lower TSMC's customer concentration and could actually help with pricing power and gross margins.

LLMs.content: Google launched Gemini 4 Neon on November 18 — its fourth Gemini 4 model in seven weeks, priced at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. It debuted #1 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, scored 61 on the AA Intelligence Index at its highest thinking setting, and reportedly matched Claude Opus 5.5 on a real coding benchmark at less than half the cost per task. > 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap → Those numbers matter. But they are not the story. The story is that the leaderboard has fractured so completely that four labs can each claim #1 on a different index — and that Google is using price, not performance, as the weapon that actually moves markets. *View original announcement on Google Blog →* ## Four Models, Seven Weeks Here is what Google shipped in the Gemini 4 family since late September: | Model | Date | Role | Pricing (per 1M tokens) | |---|---|---|---| | **Gemini 4 Argon** | Sep 30 | Deep reasoning, frontier intelligence | $2 / $10 (intro) → $4 / $20 after Nov 30 | | **Gemini 4 Carbon** | Oct 28 → Nov 10 (GA) | Most complex work, cybersecurity | $2 / $10 (intro) → $4 / $20 after Nov 30 | | **Gemini 4 Hydrogen** | Nov 12 | Speed tier, cheapest frontier | $1.50 / $0.75 | | **Gemini 4 Neon** | Nov 18 | Coding agents, knowledge work | $3 / $15 | That is a new model roughly every 12 days. No other lab has matched this shipping velocity in 2026. Anthropic's last major release was Claude Opus 5.5 on September 22 — nearly two months ago. OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17, the day before Neon, and the consensus across YouTube and Substack is that it "got slept on." We covered the Carbon/Hydrogen double-launch last week. The pattern continues: Google is not trying to win one benchmark cycle. It is trying to make the benchmark cycle irrelevant by shipping faster than anyone can evaluate. ## The Pricing Game The benchmarks are close enough to argue about. The pricing is not. Artificial Analysis measured the cost per Intelligence Index task across effort levels: | Model | Effort | Index Score | Cost/Task | Time/Task | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Gemini 4 Neon** | Low | 44 | $0.75 | 3.7 min | | **Gemini 4 Neon** | High (default) | 60 | $3.74 | 14.8 min | | **Gemini 4 Neon** | Xhigh | 61 | $6.44 | 21.5 min | | **Claude Opus 5.5** | Low | 35 | $0.98 | 3.0 min | | **Claude Opus 5.5** | High | 52 | $3.46 | 9.2 min | | **Claude Opus 5.5** | Max | 59 | $10.04 | 25.7 min | At the default settings that most developers actually use, Neon scores 60 at $3.74 per task. Claude Opus 5.5 scores 52 at $3.46. Neon delivers 15% more intelligence for 8% more money. At maximum effort, the gap widens — Neon hits 61 for $6.44 while Opus reaches 59 for $10.04. That is a 36% cost premium for two fewer index points. *View original article on The Neuron →* The Neuron's cost analysis puts it even more starkly: on the Coding Agent Index, Neon in Google's Antigravity CLI costs $6.86 per task versus $15.47 for Claude Fable 5.2 in Claude Code. That is 56% cheaper for a one-point advantage on the coding index (59 vs 58). > 💡 Google's pricing pattern is becoming clear: launch at an aggressive introductory rate, let developers build on it, then normalize upward. Argon and Carbon both started at $2/$10 and jump to $4/$20 on December 1. The question is whether Neon's $3/$15 is permanent or another intro hook. The cached input rate — $0.15 per million tokens, a 95% discount — is where the subsidy becomes structural. For agentic workloads that repeatedly reference the same codebase or document context, effective input costs approach zero. This is not a competitive move against Claude's pricing. AI Product.content: # How to Build an AI Adoption Roadmap for Your Company Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how companies operate, make decisions, serve customers, and manage everyday business activities. From automating repetitive tasks to analyzing large amounts of data, AI offers organizations new opportunities to improve productivity and business performance. However, adopting AI is not as simple as purchasing a subscription to an AI tool or introducing a chatbot into your workplace. Successful AI adoption requires a clear business strategy, the right technology, employee training, reliable data, and proper risk management. Without a structured approach, companies may invest in AI solutions that fail to deliver meaningful results, create unnecessary operational complexity, or introduce security and privacy risks. This is why developing an AI adoption roadmap is important. An AI adoption roadmap gives your organization a practical plan for identifying opportunities, selecting suitable AI technologies, preparing employees, implementing pilot projects, measuring results, and expanding successful solutions. Whether you run a small business, manage an established company, or lead an IT department, this guide explains how to build an AI adoption roadmap for your company step by step. At DFW IT Career, we recognize the importance of developing practical AI knowledge as businesses increasingly explore intelligent technologies. Our **AI and technology training programs** help learners develop skills relevant to today's evolving technology environment. Let's explore how your company can approach AI adoption strategically and responsibly. ## What Is an AI Adoption Roadmap? An AI adoption roadmap is a structured plan that explains how an organization will introduce, implement, manage, and expand artificial intelligence technologies across its business operations. It connects business objectives with AI capabilities and establishes a clear path from initial research to practical implementation. Rather than adopting AI tools without a defined purpose, companies use an adoption roadmap to determine: - Which business problems AI should solve. - Which departments can benefit from AI. - What data and technology infrastructure are required. - Which AI tools and platforms are appropriate. - How employees will learn to use AI. - What security and compliance measures are necessary. - How the organization will measure AI performance. - When and how successful AI projects should expand. For example, a customer support company may identify that its employees spend too much time answering repetitive customer questions. Its AI adoption roadmap could begin with evaluating customer support workflows, selecting an appropriate AI-powered assistant, testing the solution with a small team, reviewing its accuracy, and expanding it after successful evaluation. The goal is not to introduce AI everywhere. It is to use AI where it provides measurable business value. ## Why Does Your Company Need an AI Adoption Roadmap? AI technologies can offer significant opportunities, but adopting them without proper planning can lead to wasted resources and operational problems. A well-designed roadmap helps businesses make informed decisions before committing significant time and money. Here are some important reasons why companies should develop an AI adoption strategy. ### 1. Align AI Investments With Business Goals Every AI project should support a specific business objective. For example, a retail company may want to improve inventory forecasting, while a financial services company may want to identify unusual transaction patterns. An AI adoption roadmap helps decision-makers connect technology investments with measurable organizational goals. ### 2. AI Product.title: Adobe Says AI Agents Need Oversight to Deliver Real Value
AI Product.titleZh: Adobe Says AI Agents Need Oversight to Deliver Real Value
AI Product.content: For small businesses weighing whether to add artificial intelligence to everyday operations, the most important question may not be what AI can do—but how much authority it should have. Adobe is urging companies to distinguish between generative AI tools that produce content or summarize information and “agentic” AI systems that can take a series of actions across business platforms. The difference could affect how small companies handle customer service, marketing, sales follow-up and data management. In a recent Adobe analysis, the company describes agentic AI as a fit for more complex, multistep work. A traditional generative AI tool might review thousands of customer responses and identify common themes. An AI agent could go further by matching those themes with customer relationship management profiles, analytics and service records, identifying affected customer groups, and recommending—or triggering—actions in other systems. That distinction matters for small businesses because automation can deliver meaningful time savings, but greater autonomy also introduces more responsibility. **Key takeaways for small business owners:** - Generative AI may be sufficient for drafting, summarizing, brainstorming and analyzing feedback. - Agentic AI could help coordinate tasks across customer, sales and data systems. - More autonomy requires stronger data controls, permissions and human oversight. - Businesses should evaluate whether the expected savings and improved results justify the added complexity and cost. - Employees who understand the workflow should help decide where AI belongs. A small retailer, for example, could use generative AI to summarize product reviews and identify complaints about shipping delays. That may be enough if a manager simply needs a weekly report. An agentic system could be more useful if the business wants to identify which customers experienced delays, check their order histories, create targeted outreach and update records automatically. A service company could apply a similar approach. Generative AI might summarize support tickets and suggest responses. An agent could potentially classify the issue, check a customer’s contract, route the case to the right employee, schedule a follow-up and update the company’s CRM. Those capabilities could reduce repetitive work, but they also increase the consequences of an incorrect decision. Adobe says its CX Enterprise Coworker product is designed to coordinate actions across customer experience and data systems rather than treating each task separately. The company’s broader point is that businesses should match the level of AI autonomy to the work involved. “The additional autonomy needs to create enough value to justify the complexity and risk,” Adobe says. For small companies, that calculation should include more than the subscription price. Owners may need to consider integration costs, employee training, data cleanup, security reviews and the time required to monitor automated decisions. A system that works well in a demonstration may perform differently when it encounters incomplete customer records, conflicting information or unusual requests. Data reliability represents one potential hurdle. AI agents depend on accurate and accessible information. If a CRM contains outdated phone numbers, duplicate contacts or inconsistent customer categories, an automated workflow could amplify those problems instead of solving them. Permissions also require attention. An AI tool that can read customer records, change account information or send messages needs carefully defined limits. Small businesses should determine which actions require employee approval and which can happen automatically. A draft email might need only a quick review, while issuing a refund or changing contract terms may require a manager’s authorization. It now comes in **five sizes**, E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B A4B and 31B, and every one of them reads text and images and writes text. You download the weights once and run them on your own phone, laptop or server, with no subscription and no internet connection. The hard part is not getting Gemma 4. The hard part is picking the size your machine can actually hold. The names hide the memory bill. The “4B active” 26B model still needs room for all 26 billion parameters. This guide maps each Gemma 4 model to the Mac that runs it, using Google’s own memory figures. It then covers three ways to install it, its scores, how it stacks up against Qwen 3.6, and what it cannot do. ## The Key Takeaways > * **Five sizes, all free:** E2B, E4B, 12B, 26B A4B and 31B, under **Apache 2.0**, which allows commercial use. > * **Memory decides the model:** at 4-bit, Google lists **2.9GB** for E2B, **6.7GB** for the 12B and **17.5GB** for the 31B, before any context. > * **The Mac short version:** 8GB runs E2B, 16GB runs E4B or the 12B, the 26B A4B wants **24GB or more**, and the 31B is happiest at **32GB+**. > * **Strong for its size, not a frontier model:** the 31B scores **84.3%** on GPQA Diamond, but Alibaba’s own table puts Qwen3.6-27B ahead on coding, **77.2% vs 52.0%** on SWE-bench Verified. > * **Reads, does not draw:** Gemma 4 takes images (and audio on the small models) as input but only writes text, and its training data stops in **January 2025**. ## What Is Gemma 4? Infra & Chips.title: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
Infra & Chips.content: The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole. But while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there's still a paradox at the heart of Washington's AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction. The Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president's vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn't just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too. Today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global users. Chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones. The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration's dreams of AI dominance is that success at one layer of the stack is undermining its goals at another. When people hear that Chinese models are gaining users, they generally assume that those models are running on Chinese chips. While that's increasingly the case within China, the truth is that China cannot produce enough advanced AI chips to satisfy its own companies, let alone meet overseas demand. Meanwhile, America's grip on AI infrastructure is formidable. U.S. companies—Nvidia, Google, AMD, and Amazon—design nearly all deployed data-center AI chips. In cloud services, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google together control more than half of the market, with a growing cohort of U.S. "neoclouds" further extending that lead. Yet the same infrastructure that secures America's advantage in chips and cloud services gives Chinese AI models a platform to spread. Nvidia itself provides resources to help companies deploy open models—including several Chinese models—on its hardware. U.S.-based model inference providers such as Together AI, Baseten, and Fireworks serve Chinese models to users on infrastructure powered by U.S. chips. For example, DeepSeek's latest model is being offered by at least 16 inference providers headquartered outside China, including Amazon Bedrock.

Infra & Chips.content: # The Future of Nvidia: Still the AI King, But the Crown Is Getting Heavier Nvidia’s extraordinary run as the dominant force in artificial intelligence hardware shows no immediate sign of ending. Yet the company finds itself at an inflection point. Record demand collides with a sudden leadership vacuum, intensifying competition and growing questions about how long the current spending frenzy can last. The near-term outlook remains robust; the longer-term picture is more contested. In the third quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, Nvidia delivered another set of results that would once have seemed implausible. Revenue reached $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure, while data-centre sales climbed 110 per cent to $107.6 billion. The new Vera Rubin platform contributed nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments. Management guided the following quarter to approximately $130 billion and raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to around 75 per cent, from a previous 70 per cent, on a higher base. Supply commitments have swollen to roughly $390 billion and visibility into customer demand stretches into 2029 in several cases. Cloud industry backlog is reported at $2.5 trillion. These numbers explain why many analysts continue to describe the stock, even after a sharp pullback, as reasonably valued against the growth still on offer. ### The Leadership Shock The most dramatic recent development has been the resignation of founder and long-time chief executive Jensen Huang. On 12 November 2026 he stepped down with immediate effect as president, chief executive and a member of the board, after 33 years at the helm of the company he co-founded. The departure followed reports of extramarital affairs, one involving a businesswoman whom United States intelligence agencies suspected of links to Chinese intelligence, and another with a Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. The board accepted the resignation and has since stated clearly that it does not intend to reinstate him. Colette Kress, the long-serving chief financial officer, was appointed interim chief executive and continues in both roles while a permanent successor is sought. Harvey C. Jones was named the company’s first-ever board chair. For now, executives insist that operations continue as normal. The product roadmap — Rubin Ultra expected in 2027, followed by the next generation thereafter — remains intact. Whether a new permanent leader can match Huang’s combination of technical vision, salesmanship and industry relationships is the open question that will shape the next chapter. ### Competition Is Catching Up Nvidia still commands the large majority of the high-end AI accelerator market. Its CUDA software ecosystem and full-stack approach — chips, networking, systems and software — create formidable switching costs. That advantage is real and enduring. Yet the competitive landscape is shifting. Advanced Micro Devices has steadily increased its share. Hyperscalers are accelerating development and deployment of their own specialised chips: Google’s tensor processing units, Amazon’s Trainium processors and Microsoft’s custom silicon. As workloads move from pure model training towards inference and more specialised tasks, alternatives become more viable. Tools that ease the migration of models away from CUDA are improving. Export controls have already sharply reduced Nvidia’s China exposure. Further restrictions remain a risk. Power constraints, data-centre financing and customer concentration add further potential pressure points. ### The Cycle Question The most important longer-term uncertainty is the durability of AI infrastructure spending itself. Hyperscaler capital expenditure remains elevated, with the largest players collectively heading towards or beyond $1 trillion in annual outlays. Infra & Chips.title: If AI Chips Become Commoditized, Nvidia Has the Most to Lose, While These 3 Stocks Are Set to Gain
Infra & Chips.titleZh: If AI Chips Become Commoditized, Nvidia Has the Most to Lose, While These 3 Stocks Are Set to Gain
Infra & Chips.content: The AI chip market is starting to shift, and with it, **Nvidia**'s (NASDAQ:NVDA) grip. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model could start running part of its AI models on alternative AI chips to Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a process that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. This greatly reduces Nvidia's CUDA moat at a time when competitors are starting to catch up. **Alphabet**'s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) have started to outperform Nvidia's GPUs on a performance-per-dollar basis, according to Semianalysis (though some dispute the results). Meanwhile, **Advanced Micro Devices**' (NASDAQ:AMD) GPUs continue to gain traction. The company has improved its software stack, and its chips' larger memory capacity makes them ideal for inference. *Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout.* Continue » Image source: Getty Images. If the gap between AI chips continues to shrink and AI models can be quickly shifted to run on any AI accelerator, this is very bad news for Nvidia. Not only will the company continue to lose market share, but, more importantly, its pricing power will erode, and its margins will shrink. The Nvidia premium can be seen in its gross margins, which are in the mid-70% range, versus AMD's in the mid-50% range. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of **SpaceX** (NASDAQ:SPCX), have been developing their own custom AI chips to try to break free of Nvidia's high prices. All is not lost for Nvidia, as the company still holds some advantages. It has created a cohesive hardware, software, and networking ecosystem that should still be able to command a premium. It also has major current supply chain advantages, having locked up more access to constrained high bandwidth memory (HBM) supply and having more manufacturing and packaging capacity with **Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing** (NYSE:TSM). That will help it maintain its leadership position, even as it will likely face continued market-share and pricing pressure. While Nvidia may struggle, these three AI stocks look set to benefit. ## Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Lower AI accelerator prices and more Nvidia GPU alternatives could boost overall AI chip demand, which would benefit Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. It would also lower TSMC's customer concentration and could actually help with pricing power and gross margins.
